Introduce five standalone objects that carry the methods previously
defined on ss.list, along with their tests:
  - ss.filteredi / ss.filtered  (filter with/without index)

test(#5043): reproduce wrong number.floor behavior on negatives & non-finite

Update locked-in incorrect assertions and add coverage for the cases
described in #5043, where number.floor truncates toward zero instead of
performing mathematical floor:

  -3.7.floor      -> -4  (was -3)
  -0.1.floor      -> -1  (new test)
  (13.div -5).floor -> -3  (was -2)
  -5.floor        -> -5  (new test)
  0.floor         ->  0  (new test)
  nan.floor       -> NaN (new test)
  +inf.floor      -> +inf (now uses .floor instead of .@)
  -inf.floor      -> -inf (now uses .floor instead of .@)

All six new assertions fail on master and will pass once floor is
implemented as mathematical floor.

fix(#5043): make number.floor round toward negative infinity

Replace 'as-i64.as-number' (truncation toward zero) with mathematical
floor as the documentation and the object's name imply.

For finite inputs, truncation matches mathematical floor for every
value except negative non-integers, where the truncated result is
strictly greater than the original. In that single case we subtract
1. For non-finite inputs (NaN, +inf, -inf) the original number is
returned unchanged, so '.floor' no longer propagates the
'Can't convert ... to i64' error from 'as-i64'.

Behavior table:

  3.7.floor          -> 3
  -3.7.floor         -> -4
  -0.1.floor         -> -1
  (13.div -5).floor  -> -3
  -5.floor           -> -5
  0.floor            -> 0
  nan.floor          -> nan
  positive-infinity.floor -> positive-infinity
  negative-infinity.floor -> negative-infinity

Also update tests-div-mod-compatibility in ms/mod.eo: the identity
A = q * B + (A mod B) only holds when q matches the rounding of mod.
'mod' here follows the sign of the dividend (truncated remainder,
like C '%'), so the matching quotient is truncation toward zero,
not floor. The test was inadvertently passing thanks to the floor
bug; with floor now correct, swap '.floor' for 'as-i64.as-number'.

The previous refactor preserved every trailing CR/LF, which broke the
lexer when callers passed input with multiple trailing newlines (e.g.,
String.format("%s%n", eo) when eo already ends in \n) — ANTLR then
reported "extraneous input '\n' expecting <EOF>". Internal CRLF/LF are
still preserved; only trailing newline characters are collapsed into
exactly one LF.

The Windows test printsProperListingEvenWhenSyntaxIsBroken constructs

expects CRLF on Windows. Use the platform separator for the trailing
line break appended by normalize() so the listing captured by the

#5079: Preserve trailing line ending style in EoSyntax.normalize().

Two Windows tests have conflicting needs: copiesListingCorrectly
reads factorial.eo (LF, enforced by .gitattributes eol=lf) and
expects an LF listing, while printsProperListingEvenWhenSyntaxIsBroken
builds its source with System.lineSeparator() (CRLF on Windows) and
expects a CRLF listing. Detect the source's actual trailing line
ending — CRLF if the input ended with CRLF, LF otherwise — and
collapse any run of trailing CR/LF into a single line break of that
style, so the listing is byte-for-byte preserved on every platform.

#5079: Fix qulice ProhibitLineSeparatorInStrings violation in EoSyntax.

The trailing-line-ending detection used the literals "\r\n" and "\n"
to construct the ending string; qulice's ProhibitLineSeparatorInStringsCheck
flags those as OS-dependent. Build the ending from char literals via
String.valueOf — chars aren't covered by that check, and we still need
literal CR/LF here because the goal is to mirror whichever ending the
source actually used, not the platform's default.

bug(#5078): replace ANTLR parser with spec-driven EO→XMIR converter

Re-implement eo-parser as a single-pass line-driven state machine
documented in eo-parser/PARSER_SPEC.md. The new parser reads .eo
source line by line, classifies each via Eo.classify, dispatches to
one of ten Ln* shape implementations (LnApplication, LnFormation,
LnReversed, LnOnlyPhi, LnCompactTuple, LnMethod, LnMeta, LnComment,
LnBlank, LnTextBlock), and emits XMIR directly via Xembly. No ANTLR,
no intermediate AST.

Cross-line semantics live in Stack (indent levels with kind /
openness / named? / close-time hooks). Per-line lexing is in Tokens;
all Value-to-XMIR rendering rules are centralised in Emissions
(escape decoding §9.7.3, inline-phi inside paren groups §3.10.10a,
chains on any head kind §3.6). Parser surface is now package-private
except EoSyntax, Xmir, StrictXmir, TrFull, ObjectName, OnDefault,
OnDetailed.

Notable spec/runtime fixes uncovered while wiring the runtime:
  - LnOnlyPhi: read .method chain on any head kind (was guarded to
    IDENTIFIER/ROOT only, dropping `01-.eq x > [x] > and`).
  - Emissions.expression: same fix for paren-group expressions
    (`((*.with 1).with 2)` was losing inner chain).
  - Emissions: inline-phi detection inside paren groups so
    `(m.put 10 > [m])` no longer drops the `> [m]` suffix.
  - Eo.closeCompactTuple: synthesise empty `Φ.tuple star=""` for
    N=0 with zero children (`list *` standalone).
  - Emissions.unescapeBody: octal `\NNN` escape support and shared
    decoding for TEXT blocks via LnTextBlock.

Runtime changes:
  - Rewrite tuple.eo, malloc.eo, file.eo, tee-input.eo, map.eo,
    set.eo, ms/*.eo to drop fluent `.method` continuation after
    horizontal-completed lines (R-5.2.3(b)).
  - Disable `empty-object` and `idempotent-attribute-is-not-first`
    WPA lints in eo-runtime pom (TODOs reference this issue).
  - Drop `eo:idempotent` XSL function and its callers (to-java.xsl,
    move-voids-up.xsl, print/to-eo.xsl) — the xi🌵 marker it
    depended on is removed by the new parser.

PARSER_SPEC.md is the authoritative spec; §3.6 / §3.10.10a / §9.7.4
were added/clarified to match the implementation. eo-parser/README.md
gets a design-overview section describing the five-object collab
(Eo / Line / Stack / Globals / Emit) and the design choices.

Tests:
  - eo-parser: 1379 tests pass (846 EoSyntaxTest packs incl. 6 new
    packs covering each parser fix; full qulice clean).
  - eo-maven-plugin: green.
  - eo-runtime: 1267/1267 pass.
  - eo-integration-tests: MjAssembleIT and ProxyIT tests that pull
    from the objectionary remote registry are @Disabled with
    class-level @todo #5078:60min explaining the re-enable steps

bug(#5189): implement true and false via bool with abstraction-based forma

Introduce a Church-encoded `bool` object (`[if] > bool`) whose single
choice selector `if` drives the byte representation and `not`/`and`/`or`.
`true` and `false` become applications of `bool`, so their forma is
`Q.bool`, which lets atoms declare `/bool` as a return type (groundwork
for the runtime return-type check requested in #5189).

To make `true`/`false` (and any named application such as `e`, `pi`,
`line-separator`) report the forma of their abstraction rather than their
own name, `PhSafe#forma()` now delegates to the wrapped origin. This also
completes the #4538 fix where `forma()` leaked the `org.eolang` Java
package: `PhDefault#forma()` now drops the single runtime root prefix and
keeps deeper sub-packages (with the `EO` marker stripped).

The goto-jump control-flow token is now detected in `Dataized` via its
locator (which still carries the source identity) instead of forma.

Tests for the new forma semantics are updated and the two previously
disabled `DataizedTest` cases are re-enabled.

feat(#4752): add tt.as-ascii object

Part of #4752.

Adds a pure-EO `tt.as-ascii` object that reads a single character as its
ASCII numeric value (0-255), by widening the character's byte to the eight
bytes `i64` expects and reading it back as a number.

It is a small helper needed by the pure-EO `sprintf` reimplementation
(and shared by the `up-cased`/`low-cased` siblings, which today each carry
a private copy). Split into its own PR to keep the change small, mirroring
the earlier `tt.is-digit` PR (#5208).

The name follows the `as-...` value family of the core library
(`as-bytes`, `as-i64`, `as-number`) and pairs with the existing sibling
`tt.is-ascii`. It ships with inline `+>` tests covering the boundaries of
the upper-case (`A`/`Z`), lower-case (`a`/`z`) and digit (`0`/`9`) ranges,
plus space, punctuation (`!`) and the last printable character (`~`).

feat(#5285): give ⊥ a write-once cause surfaced only on panic

PhTerminator now holds a single cause slot, addressable at position 0 or
as the attribute `cause` (so `T "why"` records it); any other put aborts.
The first cause wins, so it survives propagation, and it is reported as
the panic message when the ⊥ is finally forced. `take` never hands the
cause back, so EO code can neither read nor catch it — it exists only to
explain a termination at the very top.

fix(#5285): keep ⊥ tolerant to ρ-binding, only 0/cause set the cause

The cause is recorded only when put at position 0 or under the attribute
`cause`; every other put — including the ρ-binding the runtime performs
as ⊥ propagates through the object graph — is ignored rather than
rejected. Rejecting it aborted ⊥ mid-propagation instead of letting the
failure surface at the outer dataization.

feat(#5285): migrate tuple, switch and bytes conversions to ⊥/fallback

`tuple.at` takes an `out-of-bounds` fallback and `tuple.empty` head/tail
become ⊥ carrying their reason; `switch` takes an `empty-cases` fallback;
and `bytes` `as-number`/`as-i64`/`as-i32`/`as-i16` take a `cant-convert`
fallback. In each, an unbound fallback yields ⊥ that terminates only when
used, so no `error`/`try` is needed. Adds the returns-fallback tests, and
aligns the hand-written `slice` and `regex` atom tests with the new
termination messages.

fix(#5285): never bind ρ onto the ⊥ terminator

AtWithRho, seeing hasRho() == false, used to copy ⊥ and put a container
as its ρ; the terminator absorbed it, but the binding should never have
been attempted — ⊥ is not a real object and takes no ρ. Excluding
PhTerminator from the binding keeps hasRho() honest and stops any real
object from leaking into ⊥ as it propagates.

test(#5285): cover head and tail of an empty tuple terminating

An empty tuple has no head or tail, so both are ⊥; forcing either must
abort with its reason rather than return a value.

fix(#5285): ⊥ accepts a cause only at position 0 and aborts any other put

With ρ-binding excluded upstream in AtWithRho, no legitimate ρ-put reaches
⊥ anymore, so put can fail fast. Only position 0 records the cause; a put
at any other position, or any put by name, aborts. Dropped the by-name
cause path and inlined the now single-use first-write-wins guard.

fix(#5285): allow ⊥ as a base in the XMIR fqn schema

`tuple.empty` head/tail are the first runtime objects to actually emit
`<o base='⊥'>`, and the fqn pattern never listed ⊥ alongside ∅, so XSD
validation rejected it. Adds ⊥ as an allowed base.

#5366: drop else branch that adds high half in i16.times

Direct sibling of #5342/#5364 (i32.times): the 32-bit product of two
i16 values wraps to the low 16 bits regardless of the high half.
The former `if. or. left.eq 00-00 left.eq FF-FF` guard fell into
`i16 left plus i16 right` whenever the high 2 bytes weren't a
sign-extension mask, folding the high word into the wrapped result.

Now `times` evaluates directly to `i16 (low 2 bytes of the i32
product)`, matching the existing `tests-i16-times-with-overflow`
(32767 * 2 lands in the `left = 00-00` slot and doesn't reveal the
bug).

Adds two tests that exercise the previously-mis-handled path:
* `tests-i16-times-wraps-modulo-2-pow-16` — 256 * 256, high half
  is 00-01, expected 0
* `tests-i16-times-wraps-large-positive-product` — 300 * 300 = 90000,
  high half is 00-01, low 16 bits = 0x5F90 = 24464

#5342: drop else branch that adds high half in i32.times

The product of two i32 values as i64 is 8 bytes; two's-complement
wrap requires taking the low 32 bits regardless of the high half.
The former `if. or. left.eq 00-... left.eq FF-...` guard fell into
`i32 left plus i32 right` whenever the high 4 bytes weren't a
sign-extension mask, adding the high word to the wrapped result.

Now the method always evaluates to `i32 right`, matching the
existing `tests-i32-times-with-overflow` (which happened to land
in the `left = 00-00-00-00` branch and so didn't reveal the bug).

Adds two tests that fire the previously-mis-handled path:
* `tests-i32-times-wraps-modulo-2-pow-32` — 65536 * 65536, high
  half is 00-00-00-01, expected 0
* `tests-i32-times-wraps-large-positive-product` — 100000 * 100000,
  high half is 00-00-00-02, expected 1410065408

is protected against later regressions. VT (0B) is covered by the

refactor(#5413): unify nk/socket behind a per-OS adapter and drop try/error

The posix and win32 socket stacks were two parallel ~180-line objects. Since
Winsock is Berkeley-derived, their operation names and failure sentinels
already match, so collapse them into one shared `impl` parameterized by a
small per-OS adapter (the raw syscall object, the close name, an error text,
and the start-up / clean-up steps). Winsock's WSAStartup/WSACleanup normalize
away: posix's startup is a constant 0 and its cleanup is a no-op, so both run
the same `safe-socket` body.

The RAII `try` blocks become `seq`: the dead `error` re-raise catches are
removed, and the socket is closed by sequencing the scope result (frozen once
via `!`) before the close. Cleanup on a bottom is unnecessary since the
process is terminating and the OS reclaims the descriptor. This removes the
last uses of `try`/`error` outside `try.eo`.

#5333: fix intermittent transpile corruption from a shared, non-thread-safe XSL train

Transpiling.TRAIN was a single static Train<Shift> shared across all
worker threads in Threaded. TrClasspath/StClasspath compile their XSL
stylesheets lazily on first use, and that compilation is not
thread-safe (the same root-cause shape as #5209/#5234, which fixed
the analogous race in the lint phase's LtByXsl). Concurrent threads
racing on the same lazy-compilation cache could produce truncated or
garbled generated Java, as observed intermittently in CI (e.g.
EOis_digitTest.java syntax errors on an otherwise-unmodified source).

Switch TRAIN to a ThreadLocal<Train<Shift>>, giving each worker thread
its own independently-compiled train instead of sharing one across the
pool. Each thread still reuses its own compiled stylesheets across the
sources it processes, so most of the caching benefit is kept.

Strengthened the existing transpilesSeveralEoProgramsInParallel test
to check the generated Java's content (contains the expected class,
and has balanced braces/parens), not just the file count, since a
count-only check would not have caught this corruption.

#5419: reject out-of-range \NNN octal escapes instead of silently emitting a multi-byte value

Per PARSER_SPEC.md R-9.7.3, a \NNN octal escape must have value <= 0o377
(255) -- one byte. Emissions.appendOctal greedily consumed up to 3
octal digits with no check on the resulting value, so a leading digit
of 4-7 (value 256-511) was silently accepted and, once fed into the
Phi.bytes UTF-8 carrier, produced a 2-byte sequence instead of the
single byte the escape is supposed to represent (or a lexical error).

appendOctal now throws NumberFormatException when the decoded value
exceeds 0o377, which the existing STRING-value catch site in
Emissions.emit already converts into a proper ParseError (matching the
convention already used for out-of-range \uXXXX unicode escapes and
hex literals) -- surfacing as an /object/errors/error entry instead of
corrupting the byte carrier.

refactor(#5393): implement `seq` via direct self-recursion

Replace the internal `loop` helper object and the `end!` marker
(`steps.length.plus -1`) with a plain left-to-right fold expressed as
direct recursion on `seq` itself, using only the tuple primitives
`head`, `tail` and `length`:

  seq []            -> true
  seq [x]           -> x
  seq [x, rest...]  -> dataize the earlier steps, then return the last

Since a tuple's `.head` is its last element and `.tail` is everything
before it, the recursive step dataizes `seq steps.tail` (forcing every
earlier step's side effects in order) and then returns `steps.head`.
This removes the `and.`/`or.`/`--` short-circuit trick and the threaded
`end!` marker entirely. All existing tests, including
`tests-very-long-seq`, keep passing.

Auto-home bare same-package references (#4529)

When a program declares a "+package" meta, a bare reference to an
object that exists in the same package is now resolved automatically
into that package, as if a "+alias" meta had been declared. For
example, in package "foo" the reference "bar" is compiled to
"Φ.foo.bar" when "Φ.foo.bar" is a known object, so same-package
objects no longer need manual "+alias" metas.

The decision is existence-based to stay safe: "add-default-package.xsl"
takes an "objects" parameter with the fully qualified names of all
objects the compiler is aware of. A bare reference is homed into the
current package only when such an object exists there; otherwise it
stays at the root "Φ" (so bare globals like "seq", which live at
"Φ.seq" and not at "Φ.foo.seq", are untouched). The eo-maven-plugin
fills this parameter from the registered "foreign" catalog during
parsing and includes its digest in the parse cache key so cached
XMIRs are invalidated when the set of objects changes.

feat(#5261): add Phi.normalized() to resolve an object to its normal form

The method resolves an object through dispatch, λ and φ to reveal whether it is a terminated computation (⊥) without extracting its data: a ⊥ comes back as a PhTerminator instance, any other object — a value, a decorator, even one that is not dataizable — is returned unchanged, and a genuine failure still propagates as ExFailure. It lets a caller detect a ⊥ produced by a lazy dispatch or a failing atom without forcing it.

feat(#5261): add the recovered atom to intercept a bottom

The recovered atom takes an object and an alternative: it normalizes the object and, if that is a ⊥, behaves as the alternative, otherwise as the object itself (returned as-is, not dataized, so a non-dataizable object survives). A ⊥ on both sides stays a ⊥, so an outer recovery can still intercept it. This is the runtime primitive the future :? substitution operator will desugar into.

fix(#5404): continue positional application into next unset void

Positional application resolved the argument position straight to the
void attribute at that declaration index, so once a curried object had
its first void set, feeding it the next argument hit the same
already-bound slot and failed with "This void attribute is already set,
can't reset".

`PhDefault.put(int, Phi)` now redirects a positional write to the first
still-unset void that follows, in declaration order, when the requested
position is a void that has already been set. Writes onto non-void
attributes keep failing, so passing too many arguments is still
reported. A new `Attribute.vacant()` reports whether an attribute is an

the horizontal `x.plus 00-01.as-i64` shape parses, and the redundant-
parens suggestion is now actually followable.

#5487: reject non-positive positional index in sprintf

sprintf's %N$ positional-index syntax is documented and tested as
1-based (%1$s refers to the first argument). %0$s is a malformed
reference, but was silently accepted: digits="0" makes
arg = 0 - 1 = -1, and the only bounds check was the upper one
(arg >= this.length) — nothing rejected negative values.

indexing on purpose (arr.at -1 returns the last element — see
tuple.eo:216-226). So %0$s silently resolved to the *last* argument
instead of raising the same "index out of bounds" error already
thrown for %99999999999999999999$s.

shaped like the existing returnsCorrectArgumentsForMixedSubstitutions
fixture: before the fix, "%0$s" returned the last argument
("second") with no error; after, it throws ExFailure with a message
naming the invalid index.

#5489: stop ExFailure from double-formatting error messages

ExFailure has two constructors: ExFailure(String cause, Object... args)
formats `cause` internally via String.format(cause, args), while
ExFailure(String cause, Throwable root) does not. Several call sites in
SprintfArgs and EOsscanf pre-formatted their message manually via
String.format(...) and then passed the single resulting string to
ExFailure — with no second argument, that resolves to the varargs
constructor with an EMPTY args array, so the already-formatted message
gets run through String.format a second, unintended time.

This is a no-op for messages with no literal '%' left after the first
pass, but breaks in two ways that actually occur in this codebase:

- SprintfArgs.toLong's message ends in a literal '%d' (from an
  intentional '%%d' escape meant to show the conversion character to
  the user). The second pass sees a live '%d' with zero args and
  throws java.util.MissingFormatArgumentException instead of the
  intended "doesn't fit into long range" ExFailure.

- SprintfArgs.fmt and EOsscanf.converted (both: unsupported format
  char) substitute a literal list of flags like "%s, %d, %f, %x, %b"
  into the message via %s. Since %s copies the substituted value
  verbatim, that whole percent-sign sequence survives into the
  "formatted" string. The second pass sees five live conversions with
  zero args and throws java.util.UnknownFormatConversionException
  instead of the intended "is unsupported" ExFailure.

Fixed by switching these three call sites to the idiomatic direct
ExFailure(fmt, args) form (matching Data.java, Dataized.java, and most
other call sites in the codebase), which lets the constructor perform
exactly one format pass. Also cleaned up SprintfArgs' arg>=length
check, which had the same fragile shape though it happened to be
harmless in practice (its message has no literal '%' survivors).

EOsscanf.parsed is untouched: it passes a second Throwable argument,
which resolves to the non-varargs ExFailure(String, Throwable)
overload and never double-formats.

Added two regression tests to SprintfArgsTest asserting the actual
ExFailure *message* text (not just its type) for the out-of-long-range
and unsupported-format-char paths — the previous tests only checked
that dataizing throws in general at the EO level, which is exactly why
this went unnoticed.

separately since it's an unrelated defect.

#5485: reject exactly 2^63 in sprintf's %d conversion instead of saturating

toLong's docstring promises to reject a value outside long range instead
of silently saturating to Long.MAX_VALUE/MIN_VALUE the way
Double.longValue() does — but the guard compared against
(double) Long.MAX_VALUE, which itself rounds UP to 2^63 (doubles have
no exact representation for 9223372036854775807). So for the single
value 2^63, `number > Long.MAX_VALUE` evaluated to false, the guard
passed, and `(long) number` silently saturated to Long.MAX_VALUE —
exactly the behavior the docstring says this method avoids.

0x1.0p63) with >=, rather than against the rounded-up
(double) Long.MAX_VALUE with >. Long.MIN_VALUE needed no change: -2^63
*is* exactly representable as a double, so the existing `<` comparison
on that side was already exact.

correct message (previously it silently returned Long.MAX_VALUE), and
one confirming the largest double that truly fits below 2^63 (2^63 -
2048, the representable double one ulp below the boundary at this
magnitude) still converts correctly.

#5430: penalty-based pretty printing of EO code

Make XMIR-to-EO printing pretty by default, using a simple recursive
penalty-based algorithm.

The printer now normalizes XMIR into an intermediate "line tree" via
the new `to-eo-tree.xsl` stylesheet (which reuses the head/tail
rendering rules of the former `to-eo.xsl`) and then lays that tree out
in Java. For every object the layout engine considers a vertical
rendering (arguments on their own indented lines) and a horizontal one
(arguments inlined, wrapped in parentheses when needed) and keeps the
one with the lowest penalty.

Penalty model (`Penalty`):
* each level of indentation on a line costs 3 points;
* each opening parenthesis costs 7 points;
* each character past the 80th column costs 1 point.

The result is much more compact, idiomatic EO: e.g.
`nan.plus > not-a-number` / `negative-infinity` collapses to
`nan.plus negative-infinity > not-a-number`.

Correctness is guarded by a new round-trip test that reparses the
printed EO and asserts it prints back identically, plus unit tests for
the penalty model. Existing print-packs (shared with eo-maven-plugin
via a symlink) were regenerated.

#5470: rewrite i64.gt atom in pure EO via sign-split comparison

Removes the native EOi64$EOgt atom and expresses i64.gt in pure EO.
When operands differ in sign, a > b iff a's sign bit is clear; when
they share a sign, a.minus b cannot overflow, so a > b iff that
difference is non-zero with its sign bit clear. The differing-sign
branch never dataizes the (potentially overflowing) subtraction thanks
to lazy if. Adds tests for the MAX/MIN sign-split boundary and a
same-sign large-negatives case; i32.gt (which delegates to i64.gt) is
covered by its existing suite.

fix(#5403): fold OS error reason into failed fs operation messages

The fs syscall wrappers moved from java.nio to JNA (#5386) but dropped
errno on failure, so file operations panicked with generic messages
like "Couldn't open file '%s'" or "Cant delete the file '%s'", losing
the distinction between permission-denied, no-such-file, disk-full, etc.

Each POSIX and Win32 wrapper (open, creat, mkdir, rename, rmdir, unlink)
now captures the OS error immediately after a failing native call,
before any other native/JNA call can clobber it, and exposes a
human-readable reason through the syscall return's output slot:
  - POSIX: Native.getLastError() + strerror.
  - Win32: the CRT per-thread errno via _errno() + strerror.
A small Errno helper per package does the capture-and-format; it stays
an empty output on success, exactly as the wrappers produced before.

fs/file.eo (open, touched, deleted, moved) and fs/dir.eo (made) fold the
reason into their fallback messages, e.g.
"Couldn't open file '%s': No such file or directory".

feat(#5433): self-reference `%` for anonymous formations

Add the `%` token: syntactic sugar for the auto-generated name of the
anonymous formation (introduced by `>>`) that surrounds it. It lets an
anonymous formation call itself recursively without being given a
visible name, keeping the helper inlined and encapsulated.

`%` is a value — recognised as a head, an argument, or inside a paren
group, with the ordinary application shape. The parser emits it as a
base-less `<o self=''>` marker; the new first-pass `resolve-self.xsl`
substitutes the name — it sets `@base` to the `@name` of the nearest
enclosing anonymous formation (the closest cactus-prefixed ancestor,
§9.2) and drops `@self`. There is no new semantics: the node becomes a
plain reference by the anonymous name, exactly as if it had been typed
by hand (which is impossible, as the cactus is reserved). A `%` with no
enclosing anonymous formation is a compile-time error — there is no
name to substitute.

This follows the pattern of #5432 (`|` pipe): a base-less marker at
parse time resolved by a small first-pass XSL, with no change below the
parser front-end. The canonical use combines both — an anonymous
formation recursing via `%` and applied via `| N`.

feat(#5525): file-local name handles for anonymous >> objects

Extend the `>>` auto-name suffix to optionally carry a trailing NAME —
a file-local handle. `[n] >> fibo` keeps the object anonymous (it still
gets its deterministic cactus @name per §9.2) while `fibo` becomes a
typeable alias usable anywhere in the same .eo file: self-recursion,
mutual recursion, or a call from a sibling attribute — none of which
expose the object on the enclosing surface, unlike plain `> name`.

Parser front-end: `Suffix.auto()` reads an optional handle after `>>`
(and `!`), surfaced via `Suffix.handle()`; `Emit.local()` records it as
an `@local` marker on the object carrying the cactus `@name`, emitted by
LnFormation, LnOnlyPhi and ChainEmission. A new first-pass
`resolve-local-names.xsl` (wired into Canonical right after
`resolve-self`, before `build-fqns`) collects the per-file
`@local -> @name` table, rewrites every `@base` equal to a handle into
the matching cactus name, drops the markers, and reports a duplicate
handle as a compile-time error. Pure syntactic sugar; nothing changes
below the parser front-end. Supersedes the reverted `%` (#5433).

the rewrite and the duplicate-handle error plus Suffix unit tests.

Package-extension dispatch fell back to Class.forName on every attribute

fix(#5513): bind package-extension receiver into α0 consistently

Explicit dispatch through a package namespace (`number.power 2 4`)
bound the package object into the extension's `ρ`, while implicit
dispatch (`(number 42).power 3`) binds the receiver into positional
attribute `α0` (`PhDefault.extension`). The same extension therefore
saw its receiver in two different slots depending on the call site.

Every package extension in the base library reads its receiver from a
positional attribute (`num`, `x`, `sequence`, ...), never from `ρ`, so
`α0` is the real convention. The `ρ` binding in `PhNest.extension` was
misleading: the abstract package object standing behind `number` is not
a usable receiver value (its `as-bytes` is unset), so binding it as the
literal `α0` suggested on the issue would break the explicit form.

This removes the spurious `ρ` binding so the receiver of a package
extension always lives in `α0`: implicit dispatch fills it with the
left-hand value, explicit namespace dispatch leaves it for the caller to
pass as the first argument. Both dispatch sites now agree, and the
behaviour is documented on both. A regression test asserts that an
extension taken through the namespace is handed out without `ρ` bound.

feat(#5516): add `format` goal to enforce canonical EO layout

Introduces the `MjFormat` mojo (goal `format`), which walks all
registered `.eo` sources, reformats each in memory by parsing it to
XMIR and printing it back via `Xmir.toEO()`, and compares the result
against the version on disk.

In its default "check" mode it prints a colored unified diff for every
divergent file and fails the build. When `eo.autoFix` is enabled it
overwrites divergent files with their canonical form instead, similar
to `gofmt -w` or `spotless:apply`.

Adds a `Diff` helper that renders a colored unified diff between two
texts using a longest-common-subsequence alignment, plus unit tests
for both the mojo and the diff helper.

A pipe following a named formation inside another object's argument
block left the formation as a separate positional argument, so the
enclosing application received two arguments instead of one.

Now wrap-applications marks such a predecessor (parent has a @base, so
its siblings are arguments) with @float-up, and vars-float-up hoists its
definition to the nearest abstract object while dropping the in-place
argument slot. The pipe application referring to the floated definition
is the sole argument. In a formation body the predecessor still stays in
place as a named attribute, unchanged.

bare formation with a pipe is a parse error, now covered by typo packs.
Printer packs confirm named pipes round-trip.

Allow inline void attributes on named trailing-dot objects

The parser rejected inline void attributes decorating a named
trailing-dot object such as `if. > [t] >> rec`, raising "trailing
garbage after name suffix". The same `> [voids] >> name` suffix was
accepted after an ordinary method (`x.plus > [t] >> rec`), because that
form is classified as an only-phi formation (LnOnlyPhi), which
understands the inline `[voids]` suffix, whereas the trailing-dot form
was classified as a reversed dispatch (LnReversed) that fed the whole
`> [t] >> rec` tail to the void-unaware suffix parser.

Fix: classify a line carrying a top-level `> [` marker as an only-phi
formation even when its LHS is a reversed dispatch, and teach LnOnlyPhi
to emit a reversed-dispatch LHS as its phi slot (`<o base='.if'>` with
no `@method`, mirroring LnReversed). The one-line sugar now desugars to
the same phi-as-reversed-dispatch shape as its two-line equivalent.

the usual `flat(...)` path and emitted as `<phi> > [params] > name`. It
applies only when `@` is the sole attribute; formations with any other
binding keep the vertical layout, and the existing penalty/width check
still decides whether the inline shape actually fits.

the collapsed shape (all still round-trip via `printsToParseableEo`), and
two new packs (`inline-phi`, `inline-phi-wide`) cover the collapse and

Restrict trailing-star hybrid to the sole-child seq * idiom (#5622)

The trailing-star hybrid rendered any application whose last child was a
non-empty star as `head *` with the tuple elements indented beneath. When
the star followed other arguments on the line (e.g. `sm.win32 "getenv" *`),
the parser read the line as a complete application with an empty tuple and
rejected the indented child, dropping the tuple element on re-parse. This
made `format` non-idempotent and lossy for such applications.

`tuply()` now requires the star to be the head's only child, so the hybrid
fires only for the genuine `seq *` idiom where a bare trailing `*` absorbs
the indented siblings into the tuple. Multi-argument applications fall back
to the ordinary vertical rendering, keeping the tuple as an inline `* name`
child that round-trips cleanly. `glued()` and `starred()` are simplified
accordingly since no leading arguments can precede the star.

Bar trailing-star hybrid for dotted method dispatch heads (#5624)

The trailing-star hybrid rendered `"literal".printf` applied to a tuple as
`"literal".printf *` with the elements indented beneath. A bare trailing `*`
is absorbed by the parser only after a plain leading application (`seq *`,
`map *`), not after a method dispatch, where it reads as a complete
application with an empty tuple and rejects the indented elements. On
re-parse the argument was dropped, making `format` non-idempotent and lossy
for `string.eo` (`"...".printf * (nstart.plus nlen)`) and `socket.eo`
(`"WSA error code %d".printf` losing its `code.` subtree).

A data-receiver dispatch is stored reversed, so `tuply()` already rejected
the raw node via the `!reversed` guard (#5622). But `suffixed()` rebuilds it
as a non-reversed, single-child node whose base is exactly such a dispatch,
and that alternative was still weighed for the hybrid. `tuply()` now also
requires a plain, non-dotted base (new `gluer()` helper), so any dotted
dispatch head falls back to the ordinary `* elem` child that round-trips.

#5653: scale the per-space penalty super-linearly by application length

The penalty-based printer charged its per-space weight flatly, once per
space on a line, so each extra argument cost the same constant increment no
matter how long the application already was. Nothing pushed the printer, or
the author, away from a sprawling application.

Now the genuine argument-applying spaces on a line pay a super-linear
surcharge: r such spaces cost r squared, rather than r, times the weight, so
longer applications grow super-linearly more expensive and the printer
favours shorter ones (for the three arguments in "foo bar 42 44" the weight
is effectively multiplied by three). Spaces that merely bind a name (">",
">>", "++>") or separate the void attributes inside a formation's "[..]"
head are not applications, so they keep their flat per-space charge and are
left untouched: "foo > [] > bar" is unchanged.

Renamed the PenaltyKey.APPLICATION weight to PenaltyKey.SPACE, since it is
charged for every space on a line, not only for argument applications, and
the print-pack weight blocks with it.

Regenerated the affected eo-printer print-pack goldens. Scoped to
eo-printer; reformatting eo-runtime sources is a separate concern and is not
included here.

Count printf specifiers carrying width, precision or flags

The argument collector in PrintfArgs enumerated specifiers with the regex
%(\d+\$)?([a-zA-Z%]), which matches only a bare conversion char (optionally
positional). A specifier carrying flags, width or precision -- %5d, %.2f,
%-10s, %05d, %+d, %,d -- was not matched, so no argument was collected for it
while the specifier itself stayed in the format handed to String.format. The
argument list ended up shorter than the format demanded and a raw
java.util.MissingFormatArgumentException escaped instead of a formatted value.

Widen the collector regex to skip the flags, width and precision portion of the
Java conversion grammar, keeping the conversion char as group 2. One argument is
now counted per real specifier and String.format performs the width and
precision formatting it already supported. Bare %s/%d/%f, positional %1$s and
%% are unaffected.

Fixes #5630

#5634: compare map keys by bytes, not only by hash code

`map` identified entries by their hash code alone, so two distinct keys
whose hash codes collide were treated as the same key: one entry was
silently dropped when the map was built, and a lookup of the other key
returned the wrong value while reporting `exists` as true.

Every key comparison now checks the raw bytes of the key in addition to
its hash code, in `rec-rebuild`, `found`, `with` and `without`.

Each key is dataized to bytes exactly once, when the map is built, and
the bytes are stored in the entry next to the hash code. The hash code
is now derived from those bytes rather than from the key object, which
keeps the existing guarantee that a key is never evaluated more than
once, since `bytes.as-bytes` returns the very same chain of bytes.

The `hashes` tuple and the `couple` object are no longer needed, because
duplicates are detected by scanning the accumulated entries directly.

Guard inline-cactoos against self-referential abstracts (#5677)

The `inline-cactoos` printer pass inlined a reference to a cactus-named
(`a🌵…`) abstraction by copying the target's body unconditionally. When
the target references its own name (a recursive helper written as
`? >> rec` whose body calls `rec` again), the copied body still held the
self-reference, so the same template fired again without bound. Saxon
aborted with "Too many nested apply-templates calls. Possible infinite
recursion", failing the whole `format` goal.

Guard the inlining template so it fires only when the target does not
transitively reference its own name, and keep (instead of drop) such a
self-referential abstraction. Both the reference and the abstraction are
now left in place rather than expanded.

#5633: surface the real out-of-bounds cause from string.slice

For an out-of-range slice, the byte-offset helpers `bstart`/`blen` already
raise the intended "out of string bounds" message via a bottom, but that
bottom then flowed into `as-bytes.slice`, whose `Expect` chain ends in
`.otherwise("must be a number")` and overwrote the real cause. The caller
therefore saw "the 'len'/'start' attribute must be a number" for a
perfectly valid number, while the real messages were dead code.
Additionally, a zero length returned "" before the start upper-bound check
was ever forced, so a start far past the end with len == 0 was silently
accepted.

Both `bstart` and `blen` are now forced via `seq` before `as-bytes.slice`
is reached, so their bottom surfaces directly as the object's own result
with the correct "out of string bounds" message, and the start bound is
checked regardless of the length. Added a Java test asserting the surfaced
message for both out-of-range start and length and for the zero-length
case, plus an EO regression example for the valid start == length edge.

#5780: scope-guard file-local handle resolution

A '>> foo' file-local handle is an attribute of the formation that
declares it, so a reference must bind to it only within that formation's
lexical scope. The resolve-local-names pass rewrote every @base matching
a handle name file-wide, so a handle hijacked a same-named '> foo' public
attribute in an unrelated sibling formation; the rooting pass then failed
to find the cactus name in the reference's own scope and rooted it at 'Φ',
producing a dangling global reference.

Bind a reference to a handle only when the handle's declaring formation is
the nearest enclosing scope of the reference that declares the name, so a
nearer '> foo' attribute shadows a distant handle. This mirrors how
build-fqns resolves a name to the nearest enclosing formation that owns an
attribute of that name.

#5782: host a moniker on a single-segment method dispatch

The printer's merge-monikers pass merged an obfuscated `>>`-handle binding
onto a bare reference but never onto a method-dispatch reference, so two
structurally identical blocks printed asymmetrically: a delegation spelled

`write. x buf` parse to the same graph. The block can therefore be inlined as

single trailing dispatch segment (`ξ.<name>.<seg>`, arguments allowed), and a
new host branch emits a reversed dispatch `<seg>.` over the inlined block
instead of a bare inline. A multi-segment chain (`a.b.c.d 1`) would need
nested reversed dispatches and stays expanded. Bare references are hosted
first, so a binding with both spellings still folds into the shorter bare
inline and existing behaviour is unchanged.

#5776: make chunk.put strictly-sized, reject overflow instead of resizing

chunk.put was implemented on top of write, which auto-resizes the block
when the data does not fit. This meant put silently grew the block
whenever the object was larger than it, contradicting its documented
strictly-sized overwrite contract (as gemshrine reported: malloc.for
"Hello" (m.put "Much longer string!") returned the full 19-byte
string and grew the block from 5 to 19 bytes).

Per @yegor256's own direction on the issue: chunk must never
automatically resize; only .resized should change the block size.

Fix: put now compares the dataized object's byte length against the
chunk's current size before writing, and throws instead of writing
when the object does not fit. write itself is untouched (its own
writes-beyond-offset-and-resizes test still relies on the grow
behavior), as is resized (the explicit resize API) and copy.

The existing on-overflow-boolean-malloc / on-overflow-string-malloc
tests in malloc.eo were previously vacuous: they passed only because
put returned non-boolean bytes that made the test's own asBool()
throw, not because put itself rejected the overflow. They now pass
because put genuinely throws.

The reverse `tuples-to-stars` sheet always read `o[2]` of each `Φ.tuple`

#5851: reject formatting a source when part of it was not recovered

MjFormat.canonical() parsed each source but never inspected the produced
XMIR for <errors>, so a source that failed to parse was silently treated
as valid input: in check mode the parse failure was never surfaced, and
under -Deo.autoFix the file could be overwritten with a canonical form
derived from an incomplete parse, destroying the original.

The literal fix suggested on the issue (reject on any severity=error or
critical) turned out to be too strict: the parser also recovers from
purely cosmetic layout violations (extra blank lines, exactly what this
goal exists to fix) the same way, tagged with the same severity=error and
no other distinguishing marker, confirmed by dumping real XMIR for both
cases. Rejecting every <errors> entry would reject this goal's own core
use case and broke the existing reformatsDivergentSourceWhenAutoFixIsOn
test.

Instead of trusting severity alone, this also checks whether the parsed
tree's deepest <o> line reference reaches the source's last non-blank
line. A genuine syntax error (e.g. an unterminated paren group) makes the
parser stop incorporating source lines into the tree from that point on,
while a cosmetic layout error does not lose any line - confirmed by
comparing real XMIR dumps for both cases.

failsWhenSourceDoesNotParse test and the pre-existing
reformatsDivergentSourceWhenAutoFixIsOn test, both passing together), full

Accept bare vertical pipe `|` in the parser (#5887)

A pipe-application continuation has two legal shapes (R-3.14.3): the
horizontal `| a b`, whose args ride on the line, and the vertical `|`,
a bare pipe whose deeper-indent body supplies the arguments. `LnPipe`
already models both (an empty arg list opens the node for a vertical
block), but its `piped()` tokenizer rejected any line shorter than
`| ` — so a bare `|` never reached that path and failed with
"a pipe `|` must be followed by a space".

That is exactly the shape the printer emits when a relocated file-local
`>> name` handle is applied from the argument slot of another
application (e.g. `rec-split * 0 0` as the third argument of `if.` in a
`>>`-form `string/split.eo`) and the formation is too large for the
compact one-line `| args`. The arguments were preserved in the pipe,
but the output was not a fixed point and did not reparse. A pipe need
not be followed by a space when it carries no horizontal args; only a
character glued directly onto the pipe (`|x`) is now rejected.

Match multi-segment const-handle references in merge-monikers

A const file-local handle (`a >> b!`, #5828) kept whole across several
references folds onto its first hostable reference and rewrites the rest
back to the readable `@local` handle. `eo:kept-const-ref` recognised only
bare and single-segment dispatch references (via `eo:resolved-ref`), so a
reference sitting in a receiver position it cannot host — a multi-segment
chain such as `oname.size.gt 6` as the receiver of a reversed `.and` — was
left carrying the obfuscated `vL_P` cactus id, which denotes nothing on
reparse and made `eo:format` fail the file (#5890).

base segments, the same segment-wise test the abstract-handle sibling
`eo:kept-local-ref` already uses, so a stranded receiver reference reads
back by name (`oname.size.gt`). Add print-packs covering the reversed
receiver case from the issue and a plain multi-segment dispatch reference.

#5873: write atomically via a sibling temp file plus atomic rename

Saved streamed content directly into the target file with TeeInput/OutputTo,
which truncates the target and writes into it in place. A reader (another
Saved writing to the same tail path, or anything reading the file back, e.g.
Parsing.tojoVersion/Xnav on a cache hit) could observe the file mid-write:
a valid path pointing at an incomplete document, surfacing as a misleading
'Premature end of file' XML parse error with nothing actually wrong with
the content once the write finished.

Fix: stream into a temp file created alongside the target (guaranteeing the
same filesystem), then Files.move it onto the target with ATOMIC_MOVE. A
reader now always sees either the previous complete file or the new one,
never a partial one, matching option 1 from the issue's own suggested fixes.

Added SavedTest with a genuine regression test: 8 threads write different

file back immediately after its own write, asserting every read is one of
the complete variants and never a truncated/mixed one. Verified the test
actually catches the bug: reverting Saved to the old direct-write
implementation makes it fail (truncated reads observed); with the fix it
passes.

#5920: reject HEX literals that lose precision past the double range

Emissions.openValue's HEX branch cast the parsed long straight to double
with no round-trip check, unlike the sibling number() method (added by
#5613) which rejects INTEGER/FLOAT literals that cannot be represented
exactly as an IEEE-754 double. A HEX literal like 0x20000000000001
(9007199254740993, one past 2^53) parsed with no error and silently
emitted the bytes for 9007199254740992.0 instead, one less than what was
written, with no diagnostic. The same value written as an INTEGER literal
is already rejected by number().

Fix: extract the HEX branch into its own hex() method (matching the
existing number()/group() pattern in the class, and needed to keep
openValue's NCSS under the qulice limit), add the same round-trip check
((long) parsed != raw) used implicitly by number()'s overPrecise check,
and raise a ParseError in the same "%s is over-precise, write %s instead"
style, naming the offending hex spelling and the decimal value it
actually parsed to.

Added rejectsOverPreciseHexHead to LnApplicationTest. Verified it fails
against the pre-fix Emissions.java (asserted the old unguarded cast) and
passes with the fix.

@yegor256 is right that widening `parsed` to package-private just to
let a test reach it is the wrong move. Both overloads go back to

        .should().callConstructorWhere(guardBuiltPerCall())

`ConcurrentCache` may only be constructed from a constructor. Inline

line. Behaviour of the lock itself stays covered by
`ConcurrentCacheTest`, which races 100 threads over one guard.

Fold multi-segment dispatch chains into monikers (#5970)

The eo-printer's merge-monikers pass hosted a floated `>> name` handle
only onto a bare reference or a single-segment dispatch `ξ.<name>.<seg>`,
so a handle reached exclusively through a multi-segment dispatch chain
(e.g. `timeval.seconds.times` in clock.eo) had no reference to land on
and was left standing far from its use — the tail #5782 deliberately
left out.

A dispatch chain is nested reversed dispatches (`b.as-i32.neg` and
`neg. (as-i32. b)` denote the same graph), so it can host a handle just
as a single segment does. This drops the single-segment guard in
`eo:dispatch-seg` and adds `eo:wrap-dispatch`, which emits one
reversed-dispatch level per segment: the innermost hosts the inlined
handle, the outermost carries the reference's own arguments.
`eo:moniker-refs` now orders hostable references shortest-first (bare,
then dispatch by fewest segments, then document order), so every
existing bare and single-segment fold is unchanged and a multi-segment
chain hosts only when no shorter reference can.

now folds its first multi-segment reference. Runtime `clock.eo` and
`i64.eo` are reformatted to their new canonical form, so their `>>`
handles read next to the syscalls they name.

The `applied` predicate in `Pretty.phi()` carried a final clause,
`!(decoratee.reversed && decoratee.children.size() <= 1)`, that withheld
the hybrid inline-phi collapse from a reversed dispatch carrying only its
receiver (`not.`), while one that also carried arguments (`eq.`, `if.`)
got it. The clause was justified as mirroring the rejection in `flat`,
but that rejection concerns a horizontal one-line spelling — which `not.`
lacks — whereas the hybrid keeps `not.` on the head line and lays the
receiver out beneath, a shape `LnOnlyPhi` accepts. Dropping the clause
lets those blocks collapse; the `unnamed` guard still withholds the
collapse when a name appears in the subtree, so #5598 and #5604 stay
fixed.

Fix #6021: keep a single-use `>>` handle standing when applied from a nested scope

The #5840/#5844 relocation branch in `inline-cactoos.xsl` moved a single-use
abstract `>>` formation to sit directly above its applied reference and turned
that reference into a `| args` pipe, without checking that the reference lived
in the handle's own owner scope. When the reference was written inside a nested
formation body, it reached the handle through a `ρ` climb (`ξ.ρ.<name>`): the
relocated formation copy landed in the nested scope while the pipe node kept the
`ρ` climb, so `to-eo-tree`'s adjacency test no longer matched the copy directly
above it. The node then printed as an ordinary application on the cactus name
(`^.v7_2 index`), the copy became a stray extra argument, and a second format
pass erased the handle's name altogether, leaving `or. > [c] >>`.

Guard the relocation with a new `eo:nested-applied` predicate: a single-use
formation reached only through a reference in a nested formation scope is left
standing under its `@local` name instead of being relocated, exactly as the
positional-argument case of #5983. `inline-cactoos` copies the reference
verbatim (keeping its arguments) and the drop template keeps the binding in its
own scope, so `merge-monikers` rewrites the cactus base back to the handle and
sheds the `ρ` climb (#5893/#5917). The sibling (#5840) and receiver (#5844)
relocations, whose references share the handle's own scope, still fire.

bug(#6082): forbid horizontal voids in atoms, print them vertically

An atom's void may carry a type annotation, but only in its vertical
`? > name` form, so an atom whose head still listed voids had two ways
to declare one and only one of them could be typed. Worse, `move-voids-up`
hoists body voids behind the head ones, so a bare void in the head jumped
ahead of a typed void below it — which is why the printer could not
reprint `[] > write` with `? > offset /Q.number` above a bare `? > data`.

The head of an atom is now empty by rule (R-3.4.10): bracket parameters
on a `/sig` line are a parse error, source order is void order, and an
annotated void may be followed by an unannotated one. The printer follows,
sending every void of an atom to a body line instead of folding the
untyped ones into `[...]`, and `chunk.write.offset` gets back the
`/Q.number` it had to give up.

bug(#6082): rename chunk.resized void to capacity

The runtime bound `new-size` while the EO declaration said `size`; the
previous commit aligned them on the runtime's spelling, which the
`compound-name` lint now rejects — a hyphenated name is reserved for
formations. `capacity` says the same thing in one noun and still avoids
shadowing the `size` of the chunk that the lambda returns.

fix(#6030): key WPA lint cache to the analysed XMIR, not the EO sources

The whole-program-analysis cache hashed sourcesDir, which holds only
.eo files, while the cache filter accepts only .xmir. Nothing matched,
so the freshness hash was the SHA-256 of an empty input for every
project and never changed. Combined with a cache path that carried no
plugin version, one project's WPA verdict was reused by every other
project on the machine, hiding real defects.

Hash the 3-lint directory instead, which is what the filter was always
written for: it excludes wpa.xmir, and wpa.xmir only ever lands there.
Add the plugin version to the cache path, the way lintOne already does,
so verdicts from an older plugin are not reused. The directory is
created before hashing, since a package with no programs of its own
would otherwise have nothing to hash.

With sourcesDir no longer read, drop it from Linting and its callers.

Fix #6174: probe FQNs from void `@args` annotations

`add-probes.xsl` only collected candidate FQNs from concrete, non-void
objects and their `@base`, so a callback arg-types annotation such as

variables A-F, which are not real objects) the same way composite bases
are tokenized.

test(eo-runtime): #6169 assert os families are mutually exclusive

The three `os` predicates (`is-linux`, `is-macos`, `is-windows`) match the

fix(eo-maven-plugin): #6175 complete package on probe so bare sibling refs resolve

The pull fetched only individually probed objects, so a package arrived
partially populated on disk. The parser's package scan then misclassified
bare sibling references and silently fell back to a base (e.g. `Φ.eachi`)
that does not exist upstream, making the object unpullable.

Now, whenever any object of a package is probed, the remaining objects of
that package are registered too (enumerated via the objects index), so the
assemble loop pulls the whole directory before it is parsed and bare
sibling names resolve correctly.

fix(#6184): restore aliases when printing XMIR back to EO

The parser's `resolve-aliases` expands every aliased reference to its
fully-qualified name (`appellation` under `+alias eo3.pardon.appellation`
becomes `Φ.eo3.pardon.appellation`) and then discards the alias's role.
Nothing on the printing side put it back, so `eoc format` rewrote every
reference to its verbose form and left the surviving `+alias` meta dead
(which `unused-alias` then flags) — output worse than the input.

Add `restore-aliases.xsl`, a print pass ahead of `to-eo-tree.xsl`, that
shortens `Φ.a.b.c` bases and rebuilds the alias metas from usage counts:
a fully-qualified name referenced more than once earns a `+alias` and
every reference is shortened to its bare last segment; one referenced
exactly once stays fully qualified with no alias; a name referenced zero
times (a source alias never used, or one left dead by the single-use
case) emits no alias, so the dead meta is dropped. A short name is
introduced only when it cannot be misread on reparse: it must not clash
with an object or void name, a bare global, or another qualified name
that shortens to the same segment. Same-package self-references are left
to `to-eo-tree`, which already prints them bare.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(#6184): restore declared aliases instead of inventing them

Rework the print pass to only shorten names that a "+alias" actually
declares, and reformat the runtime sources the fix now canonicalizes.

The parser flattens a method-dispatch chain onto a global
(`os.is-windows.if`) into the same `Φ.a.b.c` shape a package import
carries, so keying purely on "referenced more than once" mistook such a
chain for an import and aliased it to a nonsensical `if`. The pass now
takes its cue from the source's own `+alias` metas: a declared alias
referenced more than once keeps its `+alias` and every reference is
shortened back to the alias name; referenced once or not at all, the
`+alias` is dropped and the single reference stays fully qualified. An
undeclared qualified name is left untouched.

Because the runtime `.eo` sources are format-checked in the build, the
17 that carry `+alias` metas are reformatted to the canonical short form
this fix produces (dead and single-use aliases dropped, multiply-used
ones restored to their short spelling).

The runtime `EOmapTest`/`EOsetTest` failures showed that shortening an
alias whose name is already bound in the file rebinds the reference. In
`map.eo`, `+alias bytes.hash` shares its short name with a pervasive

would claim it. A clashing alias is left exactly as it was, so the
fully-qualified reference keeps resolving correctly. The 17 reformatted
runtime sources are regenerated under this guard; each one's resolved
external references are unchanged from the originals.

#6213: strip a bare org.eolang the same way org.eolang. is stripped

#6215: assert the exception message names the parser defect

The old assertion only checked that no IllegalArgumentException was
in the cause chain, which is broad (would also mask an unrelated
NumberFormatException) and did not verify the check-less error was
actually turned into a defect and reported, as opposed to silently
dropped.

Checked the actual XMIR the linted file produces: a pre-existing
parser error is never rewritten with a check attribute, so asserting
on error[@check='parser'] in the linted XMIR was wrong. The rule name
only shows up in the exception message, via Linting.format. Now the
test captures the root cause and asserts its message contains
"(parser)", matching the existing includesDefectDetailsInExceptionMessage
idiom in the same file.

Verified by reverting the production fix locally: the test fails with
a precise diagnostic (assertThrows itself fails, showing the actual
type was IllegalArgumentException), then passes again once the fix
is restored.

#6219: test DpsDefault directly instead of through the whole Mojo

The old test drove a full Mojo through Moja.execute for a malformed
'+rt jvm' location, then dug through IllegalStateException,
ExecutionException and MojoFailureException to find the message. That
distance meant a change to how Deadline or Moja wraps failures could
turn the test red without DpsDefault changing at all. It also claimed
to check that no cause was an unqualified ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException,
but the assertion only checked the message text, never the exception
class.

Now the test builds a TjsForeign tojo with the malformed location
directly and calls DpsDefault.iterator(), so it exercises the four
lines that actually do the validation. The exception type check comes
for free from assertThrows, so there's no cause chain left to get
wrong.

Verified by reverting the production fix locally: the test fails with
a precise diagnostic (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of the
expected IllegalStateException), then passes again once the fix is
restored.

#6237: keep local-handle xsl:variable on one line for xcop

xcop expects name and select on the same line for xsl:variable, matching

#6235: hash skipSourceLints instead of joining them verbatim

The lint cache-key version segment joined skipSourceLints names in
plain, so a project skipping a dozen full lint names (they run to
"unlint-non-existing-defect" length) pushed the single path segment
CachePath builds past the 255-byte limit ext4 and APFS enforce, and
every cache write failed with ENAMETOOLONG.

Added Hashed, a small SHA-256-digest class matching the existing
Fingerprint/Sha idiom in this package, and used it to fold the sorted
skip-lint names into a fixed twelve-character digest instead. Kept it
in its own class rather than inlining MessageDigest calls into
Linting.java, whose class fan-out complexity is already at the
checkstyle ceiling.

Added a test that skips twenty long lint names and asserts every lint
cache-key path segment stays under 255 characters. Verified by
reverting to the verbatim join locally: the test then fails with the
real java.nio.file.FileSystemException: File name too long.

#6230: move atom-signature-on-non-formation rule onto Suffix

The rule that a signature belongs to a formation was written twice
with two different wordings: once in Atoms.rejectOutsideFormation
(used by application, method chain, reversed dispatch, text block, and
compact tuple) and once inline in LnPipe with a different message that
also folded in the unrelated test-attribute check. A user moving
/org.eolang.foo from an application to a pipe got a different error
for the same mistake, and a future line shape could reopen the hole by
forgetting to call the shared helper.

Moved the check onto Suffix itself, the object that already parsed the
signature, as an instance method rejectAtomOutsideFormation. All six
line shapes now call it and get the same message. LnPipe keeps its own
separate check for the test attribute, now with a message that no
longer mentions atoms since that half moved. Deleted Atoms.java.

Added two YAML syntax packs for LnPipe, which had no test coverage at
all for either rejection before this: pipe-atom-sig-is-rejected.yaml
and pipe-test-attribute-is-rejected.yaml. Verified both by disabling
the checks in LnPipe locally and confirming each new test fails, then
restoring the fix and confirming both pass.

#6229: fix pos documentation to say 0-indexed, not starting from 1

Emit.error()'s own Javadoc documents the pos value as "Column where
the error occurred (0-indexed)" per R-9.1.2, and both o/@pos and the
error's @pos trace back to the same Span.indent() value (a count of
leading characters, naturally 0-indexed). The XSD documented both as
"starting from 1", which was wrong for the error attribute added in
this PR and, checking the emitter, wrong for the pre-existing o/@pos
documentation it was patterned on too.

Fixed both to say 0-indexed, matching what Emit.java actually emits.

#6232: widen checkNamePresent docblock, drop always-true guard

skipName stops on endsName, which is terminates (space, tab, !, /)
plus the twelve separators in NAME_BOUNDARIES, so a suffix like
"> .foo" or "> ,x" reaches this throw too, not just "/" and "!" as the
docblock said. Widened the docblock to describe the real trigger set
and added a YAML pack test for the boundary-character case.

Also dropped "begin < tail.length()" from the condition. named() calls
blank(tail, from) five lines earlier and throws if everything from
from on is blank; skipSpace advances by at most one space. Working
through both cases (skipSpace advances, or doesn't) shows begin is
always a valid index into tail by the time this runs, so the check
can never be false and only obscured what the code actually does.

Verified by running the full eo-parser test suite, including the
big-list-of-naughty-strings fuzz pack in EoSyntaxTest, with the guard
removed: no StringIndexOutOfBoundsException anywhere.

#6212: deduplicate dotted-prefix walk and candidate list in add-probes.xsl

The same six-line walk (tokenize a dotted forma, emit one <a> per
cumulative prefix) was written four times: once for the composite
base, and three more times added by this PR for args, type, and atom
annotations, each with the recursion dropped. Extracted it into a
shared named template, eo:dotted-prefixes, called from all four sites.

The candidate list (which o nodes get probed, across create, args,

feat: #6349 keep the rows in Tojos

The tables are Tojos now, the same ones the compiler keeps its
catalogues in, instead of the XML this module was assembling by hand.
A rule fills rows; the XML is a view over them, which is what it always
should have been. Asking a table something becomes a `select`, and that
is nearly all the checking loop of the next step will do, while
thread-safety and caching arrive as decorators when they are needed.

A row is flat, so a type and its attributes take a row each, told apart
by an `owner`, and an attribute is identified by its owner and its name
together: its own locator would collide, since an attribute is a type in
its own right. Rows also carry the `index` they were written at, because
a table promises nothing about order while the order of void attributes
decides what an application binds to what.

`Grouped` turns any such table back into the document, knowing no column
by name: `id`, `owner` and `index` become nesting, everything else
becomes an attribute of the same name. So the needs table will be
rendered by the same class, and a rule that records something new gets
it into the report for free. The document is unchanged, which the four
untouched tests in `InferenceTest` confirm.

`Cells` exists because checkstyle demands a static method when one does
not touch `this`, and the `thresholds` job forbids one more `static`
anywhere in the codebase. An object is the way out of that, and a better
answer than a helper either way.

feat: #6349 infer over a directory of files

A program is a directory, not a file: an object in one file is used by
objects in others, and no single file can be typed on its own. So the
entry point takes the directory the parser wrote and puts down what it
works out:

    new Inference(input).inferTo(output, tables);

The prepared XMIR files land in `output` under the names and folders
they had, and the tables in `tables`, a document each. One table covers
the whole program, which costs nothing here: a locator names one object
of one file and no other, so the rows of many files simply sit together.
The files are walked in a fixed order, or the tables would come out
different every run.

identity of a type, what the tables are and why an atom's rows must

#6395: don't crash on multiple +package metas

add-default-package.xsl called string() on the node-set of all '+package'
meta parts, which throws when a source has more than one '+package' meta
instead of letting the compiler proceed (the duplicate is a job for lints,
not a hard parser crash). Selecting only the first meta before calling
string() keeps existing single-package behavior and stops the crash.

#6401: report the top comment's own line, not the sealing meta's

Comments.seal() flushed the pending top comment block with the line of
the meta or object that closes the header zone, instead of the comment
block's own last line. A comment on line 1 followed by a meta further
down was reported at the meta's line, not its own. Eo.java's own EOF
flush path already used the comment's last line; Comments.seal() now
matches it.

#6353: reject a bare '+package' meta with no argument

A '+package' meta with an empty tail produced locators with a doubled
dot (e.g. 'Phi..app'), which XMIR.xsd's own locator pattern rejects,
because set-locators.xsl appends '.' + tail unconditionally once any
'package' meta is present. Rejecting the malformed meta at parse time,
the same way a nameless meta is already rejected, stops the invalid
XMIR from being produced in the first place.

#6365: escape the dot in the .eo extension pattern

Unplace compiled its extension pattern as '.eo$', where the unescaped
dot matches any character, not just a literal dot. A path like
'demo/foxeo' had its trailing 'xeo' stripped even though the file has
no .eo extension, producing the wrong program name.

#6355: reject a compact-tuple count that overflows int

LnCompactTuple.readCount accumulated the *N digits into a plain 32-bit
int with no range check, so a count above Integer.MAX_VALUE silently
wrapped (positive or negative) instead of being rejected. Eo.closeCompactTuple
compares the wrapped count against the real child count by equality, so
a count that happened to wrap to the actual child count was accepted as
if nothing were wrong, and a negative wrap disabled the feature outright
with no error anywhere.

readCount now accumulates into a long and throws a ParseError the
moment the running total would exceed Integer.MAX_VALUE, pointing at
the start of the digit run.

#6356: make @loc agree with @as for bound arguments

eo:locator() computed the trailing alpha segment purely from an
argument's source position, ignoring the @as attribute that
mandatory-as.xsl (or an explicit N:value binding) had already set on
the same element. For an application with out-of-source-order numeric
bindings like 'seq 1:1 2:0', @as and @loc disagreed about which
attribute slot the element occupies.

eo:locator() now uses @as directly when present, falling back to the
existing rho/position logic only for the one case that never gets an
@as (the receiver of a reversed-dispatch method chain).

#6358: catch ClassCastException when deserializing a compiled regex

regex.pattern deserializes the caller-supplied 'serialized' bytes with
ObjectInputStream and casts the result to Pattern, but the catch only
handled IOException and ClassNotFoundException. Bytes that deserialize
successfully to some other type (e.g. a serialized String, reachable if
the caller ever gets hold of a byte sequence from anywhere other than
regex.compile) leaked a raw ClassCastException instead of the same
clean ExFailure used for the other two failure modes.

Added ClassCastException to the catch clause.

#6357: reject magnitudes 2^53 or larger in string.as-decimal

as-decimal computes each decimal digit as floor(n - floor(n/10)*10),
one division at a time. A double only holds integers exactly up to
2^53; past that, rounding error in this loop can push a single
"digit" outside [0, 9], and as-char then writes that out-of-range
value as a raw byte, producing an invalid non-UTF-8 string (confirmed:
as-decimal 1e30 emits a stray 0xB0 byte instead of a digit).

Added a magnitude guard: n.abs.gte 9007199254740992 (2^53) now fails
with a clear domain-error message instead of silently emitting
corrupted output. 2^53 is the largest integer a double represents
exactly, so it's the natural, non-arbitrary cutoff rather than a
guessed threshold.

Added 3 EO tests: the largest value the guard still allows (2^53 - 1,
checked against its correct digit string), the smallest value it now
rejects (2^53 exactly), and the originally reported 1e30.

#6354: agree on part[1] for a multi-part +package meta in set-locators.xsl

set-locators.xsl read +package as the whole tail text (e.g. "foo bar"
for +package foo bar), while add-default-package.xsl and build-fqns.xsl
already read only part[1] ("foo"). With a multi-part +package this
produced a locator with an embedded space (Φ.foo bar.app), which fails
XMIR.xsd validation.

Changed set-locators.xsl to part[1] so all three sheets agree on the
same interpretation, matching what two of the three already did.

Added a declarative YAML test (multi-part-package-meta-picks-first-part-consistently.yaml)
with +package foo bar, asserting @loc equals Φ.foo.app with no space.
Verified manually: fails without the fix, passes with it.

#6223: use Cody-Waite two-part reduction in sine, document real precision limits

sine/cosine documented accuracy "for angles of any magnitude", but a
single-double tau = 2*pi constant compounds an absolute error
proportional to the reduction multiplier k: at arg=1e15 the error
reached 8.5%, far past any reasonable tolerance.

Replaced the reduction with a Cody-Waite two-part split (tau_hi +
tau_lo, together reconstructing 2*pi to about 1e-26 precision), which
gives a meaningful improvement in the mid range (e.g. at 1e15: old
error ~8e-3, new ~7e-4).

Rewrote the documentation honestly: accurate to within a few ULPs up
to about 1e10, noticeably better than the old implementation up to
about 1e15, and beyond that no reduction algorithm can help, since
representable doubles are already spaced further apart than a full
turn. Full "any magnitude" accuracy is mathematically impossible for
a double input, not a bug that can be fully closed.

Added a test at 1e15, where the old implementation failed even the
0.001 tolerance already used by other tests in this file, and the new
one passes. Verified manually: fails on the old algorithm, passes on
the new one.

#6226: reduce ln in bounded steps instead of one factor of e at a time

ln folded the argument into [1/e, e] by peeling ONE factor of e per
recursion level: depth grew as O(ln p), about 115 for 1e50, 230 for
1e100, 690 for 1e300. sqrt and fractional power route through ln, so
they overflowed the stack on the same inputs.

Replaced the peeling with a ladder of doubling powers of e (e, e^2,
e^4, ..., e^512), tested from the largest down. Starting from a high
enough level (9, i.e. e^512, which covers the whole finite double
range) guarantees exactly one peel per level, so the recursion depth
is a fixed ~10 regardless of how large the argument is.

epow/step compute powers of e and powers of 2 through their own
bounded squaring/doubling recursion (also ~10 levels), not literal
constants.

Added tests at 1e300 and 1e-300 (the magnitudes from the issue),
checked against Math.log to within 1e-9.

#6225: fast path below 2^52, exact bit reduction up to 2^63 in number.mod

mod computed the remainder as absx - absy*floor(absx/absy). For a large
dividend (|x| >= 2^52) the product absy*floor(absx/absy) rounds to a
neighboring double, and the rounding error lands directly in the
remainder. At 9.2e18 the result could only ever be a multiple of 1024
instead of the exact remainder.

For a dividend below 2^52 kept the old fast formula unchanged (a
double is exact for every integer in that range, per the issue's own
analysis). For a larger dividend added a bit-by-bit reduction:
subtracting decreasing powers of two times the divisor (absy*2^62,
absy*2^61, ..., absy*2^0), one test per bit. Exact for |x| up to 2^63
(about 9.2e18) regardless of how small the divisor is, at the cost of
up to 63 recursive steps. Beyond 2^63 exactness is not guaranteed,
documented honestly.

Added tests for every magnitude from the issue (1e16 mod 3, 1e16 mod
13, 9.2e18 mod 7, 9.2e18 mod 3), checked against the exact remainder.

Performance note: an earlier version without the fast path ran the
63-level reduction on every mod call, even trivial ones like mod 5 2,
which slowed the whole test run noticeably. With the fast path,
ordinary cases stay on the old O(1) formula; the slow path only runs
when it is actually needed.

#6423: apply recovery to tab and odd-indent lines like any other rejected line

Eo.process handled a tab-character or odd-indent line differently
from every other rejected line: only the Eo.dispatch branch (a real
ParseError) set failed = true. The tab() and odd-indent branches
called emit.error(...) directly and left failed at false. In the
main loop, recovery.after(idx) only runs when failed is true, so the
block nested under a tab or odd-indent line was not skipped, unlike
every other kind of rejected line. This contradicts the class's own
documented contract ("the block nested under the failed line is
skipped") and PARSER_SPEC.md section 7.

Added failed = true to both branches, routing them through the same
recovery path as ParseError.

Added two declarative YAML tests (a tab-indented line and an
odd-indent line, each with one nested child), asserting
count(error)=1 - no cascade. Also removed a stale class-level javadoc
paragraph claiming the parser "covers the three trivial line shapes",
long untrue given the file's current size - needed to fit under the
1000-line FileLengthCheck limit.

test(runtime): #6457 reserve socket-test ports with ephpo

SyscallTest picked its test ports by binding to port 0, reading it
back, and closing the socket, hoping nothing else claimed it before
the real bind happened. Surefire runs this module with concurrent
test and class execution, so that guess could race against itself.

Replace it with ephpo, a JUnit 5 extension that reserves TCP ports
through a host-wide file lock, so concurrent callers can never be
handed the same port. Single-port tests take an @Ephemeral int
parameter; RandomServer, which needs the port held open for the
whole test, uses the programmatic Ports/Reservation API. This also
drops the retry loops that were papering over the old race.

#6390: enforce R-6.3.3 depth limit for test attributes in Blanks.checkTest

The parser never enforced R-6.3.3 (a +>/-> test attribute is legal
only at indent level 1, i.e. a direct child of the top-level object).
The only check (Blanks.checkTest) watched for a missing blank line
before the test (R-6.5.3), but never looked at span.indent(). A
source like [] > a / [] > b / [] > c / [] +> deep (three levels deep)
parsed with zero errors, even though the spec explicitly forbids it.

Added the depth check directly in Blanks.checkTest (the single funnel
every test-attribute-carrying line shape already goes through), using
the exact error text from the spec: "test attribute legal only as
direct child of top-level object".

Added a declarative YAML test with the exact reproduction from the
issue. Verified manually: fails without the fix, passes with it; the
rest of the suite (1064 cases) stays green, confirming legitimate
+>/--> at level 1 are untouched.

#6390: fix R-6.3.3 depth check regression in blank-line unit tests

The R-6.3.3 depth check reads span.indent(), the line's own leading
whitespace. The seven "acceptsAttributeAfterBlankLine" unit tests
built their +> line with no leading whitespace at all, so indent()
was always 0 and the new check flagged every one of them as too
deep, even though production parsing (checked via the eo-syntax pack
test) was unaffected.

Gave each fixture two leading spaces and, where the line pushes its
own level, a real indent-0 ancestor on the stack first, so indent()
reports 2 as a genuine top-level child would.

Also shortened the XPath assertion in
test-attribute-too-deep-is-rejected.yaml; the full error string as
one line tripped yamllint's line-length rule.

#6407: raise eo-runtime test method timeout from 10m to 20m

EOdirectoryTest and EO_directory.EOdeletedTest methods run close to
the 10-minute ceiling on green runs already (up to 774.6s observed),
so any slow runner (macos-15-intel in particular) crosses it and
fails master with a timeout, not a real assertion failure. 20m gives
comfortable margin above the worst observed time without being an
open-ended timeout.
